query: Which should I use to interactively edit tabular data, st.dataframe or st.data_editor? Version unknown.

candidates.title: dataframes
candidates.section: Dataframes
candidates.text:
# Dataframes

Dataframes are a great way to display and edit data in a tabular format. Working with Pandas DataFrames and other tabular data structures is key to data science workflows. If developers and data scientists want to display this data in Streamlit, they have multiple options: `st.dataframe` and `st.data_editor`. If you want to solely display data in a table-like UI, [st.dataframe](/develop/api-reference/data/st.dataframe) is the way to go. If you want to interactively edit data, use [st.data_editor](/develop/api-reference/data/st.data_editor). We explore the use cases and advantages of each option in the following sections.

candidates.section: Edit data with st.data_editor
candidates.text:
## Edit data with st.data_editor

Streamlit supports editable dataframes via the `st.data_editor` command. Check out its API in [st.data_editor](/develop/api-reference/data/st.data_editor). It shows the dataframe in a table, similar to `st.dataframe`. But in contrast to `st.dataframe`, this table isn't static! The user can click on cells and edit them. The edited data is then returned on the Python side. Here's an example:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"command": "st.selectbox", "rating": 4, "is_widget": True},
        {"command": "st.balloons", "rating": 5, "is_widget": False},
        {"command": "st.time_input", "rating": 3, "is_widget": True},
    ]
)

edited_df = st.data_editor(df) # 👈 An editable dataframe

favorite_command = edited_df.loc[edited_df["rating"].idxmax()]["command"]
st.markdown(f"Your favorite command is **{favorite_command}** 🎈")
```

<Cloud name="doc-data-editor" height="300px"/>

Try it out by double-clicking on any cell. You'll notice you can edit all cell values. Try editing the values in the rating column and observe how the text output at the bottom changes:

candidates.title: Make `st.table` use 14px font size
candidates.section: Summary
candidates.text:
### Summary

`st.table` uses 16 px font size. Now that we use 14 px both for `st.dataframe` and for all widgets, it often looks out of place. We should change it to 14px as well.

candidates.title: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss
candidates.text:
**Request:**
I found a solution to this, but would like to know if I just use the `st.data_editor` object and corresponding `on_change` callback in a way that they were not meant to be used (passing/using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` in the callback).
-> Is there another method to handle user edits on a dataframe, which ensures that those edits are processed exactly once, so neither multiple times nor never before the Streamlit page or `st.fragment` get reloaded?
candidates.section: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss > Summary
section_path: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss

parent.title: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss
parent.text:
### Summary

**Issue Description:**

When a user edits cells in the `st.data_editor` object, the `on_change` callback function is triggered. If the user makes additional edits while the `on_change` callback is still running, some edits are processed multiple times (in this case, twice for edits of the first interaction and once for the second interaction) when using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` to process the user edits. This occurs because the callback is threaded, and the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` object still includes the edits from the previous user interaction.

**Additional Issue:**

Attempting to fix this revealed another issue: If the `on_change` callback for a previous call takes longer to execute than the latest call, the Streamlit page reloads before the previous `on_change` callbacks are finished. As a result, not all cells of the `st.data_editor` object are updated, leading to potential loss of user edits. This seems to be fixed by using `threading.Lock()` in the on_change callback function.

**Request:**
I found a solution to this, but would like to know if I just use the `st.data_editor` object and corresponding `on_change` callback in a way that they were not meant to be used (passing/using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` in the callback).
-> Is there another method to handle user edits on a dataframe, which ensures that those edits are processed exactly once, so neither multiple times nor never before the Streamlit page or `st.fragment` get reloaded?
parent.section: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss > Summary

## Edit data with st.data_editor

Streamlit supports editable dataframes via the `st.data_editor` command. Check out its API in [st.data_editor](/develop/api-reference/data/st.data_editor). It shows the dataframe in a table, similar to `st.dataframe`. But in contrast to `st.dataframe`, this table isn't static! The user can click on cells and edit them. The edited data is then returned on the Python side. Here's an example:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"command": "st.selectbox", "rating": 4, "is_widget": True},
        {"command": "st.balloons", "rating": 5, "is_widget": False},
        {"command": "st.time_input", "rating": 3, "is_widget": True},
    ]
)

edited_df = st.data_editor(df) # 👈 An editable dataframe

favorite_command = edited_df.loc[edited_df["rating"].idxmax()]["command"]
st.markdown(f"Your favorite command is **{favorite_command}** 🎈")
```

<Cloud name="doc-data-editor" height="300px"/>

Try it out by double-clicking on any cell. You'll notice you can edit all cell values. Try editing the values in the rating column and observe how the text output at the bottom changes:

candidates.title: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss
candidates.text:
**Request:**
I found a solution to this, but would like to know if I just use the `st.data_editor` object and corresponding `on_change` callback in a way that they were not meant to be used (passing/using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` in the callback).
-> Is there another method to handle user edits on a dataframe, which ensures that those edits are processed exactly once, so neither multiple times nor never before the Streamlit page or `st.fragment` get reloaded?
candidates.section: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss > Summary
section_path: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss

parent.title: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss
parent.text:
### Summary

**Issue Description:**

When a user edits cells in the `st.data_editor` object, the `on_change` callback function is triggered. If the user makes additional edits while the `on_change` callback is still running, some edits are processed multiple times (in this case, twice for edits of the first interaction and once for the second interaction) when using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` to process the user edits. This occurs because the callback is threaded, and the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` object still includes the edits from the previous user interaction.

**Additional Issue:**

Attempting to fix this revealed another issue: If the `on_change` callback for a previous call takes longer to execute than the latest call, the Streamlit page reloads before the previous `on_change` callbacks are finished. As a result, not all cells of the `st.data_editor` object are updated, leading to potential loss of user edits. This seems to be fixed by using `threading.Lock()` in the on_change callback function.

**Request:**
I found a solution to this, but would like to know if I just use the `st.data_editor` object and corresponding `on_change` callback in a way that they were not meant to be used (passing/using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` in the callback).
-> Is there another method to handle user edits on a dataframe, which ensures that those edits are processed exactly once, so neither multiple times nor never before the Streamlit page or `st.fragment` get reloaded?
